videos.script: Before anybody screws an access point to a ceiling, somebody should know where it goes, and why there. {{ceiling}} Guessing is common. One access point for every so many square metres, put in the middle of each room. It fails in ways a floor plan does not show. {{guess}} A concrete lift shaft can block more signal than thirty metres of open office. A coated glass wall that looks transparent can block more than a brick one. {{walls}} A site survey replaces the guess with measurements. It comes in three kinds. A prediction made in software, a walk that listens to what is on the air, and a walk that connects and measures what a user would get. {{kinds}} In this lesson you will compute how a signal falls with distance and with walls, using the free-space formula and a few typical losses. {{formula}} You will meet the numbers a design is judged by, and find out why minus sixty-seven dBm keeps coming up. {{target}} And you will read a heat map, which shows a great deal and hides some things that matter. {{heatmap}} The lab has no radio, so every number here is computed, and the lesson says which ones are rules of thumb. {{computed}}
